newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -JGBs unscathed by Nomura case-for now.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -JGBs unscathed by Nomura case-for now.

text.p: Japanese Government Bonds may get a boost from the latest chapter in the Nomura scandal, as bonds see the country's growing financial fragility as further reason to delay an interest rate rise, analysts said on Thursday.

With yen appreciation possible in the medium term and some players wary of a shake-out in U.S. Treasuries, international investors are starting to cast a guarded eye over the market, but remain reluctant to invest at current low yields.

"The market is perceiving things (the Nomura scandal) as positive, purely because it cements the expectation the Bank of Japan won't raise interest rates because of the fragility of the financial system," said Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International.
But there may be trouble ahead.
"The placement of bonds is not a problem at the moment because it's pretty much a liquidity driven market," said Shah.

"But if we get bad news on inflation, or the yen weakens sharply and the market expects a rate rise down the road, then it could be negative because the auctions wouldn't be supported by strong participation by the main players like Nomura."

Japan's Ministry of Finance said on Wednesday Nomura Securities and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB) would be barred from participating in the auction and underwriting of public bonds, including JGBs, municipal bonds and government-guranteed bonds, to the end of the year.
The penalties -- which followed Nomura's involvement in a raketeer payoff scandal -- extended a provisional ban already in effect since May.
Dick Howard, senior economist at Bank Julius Baer, said if there were to be any fall-out from the Nomura affair, it would be to push JGB prices down.
"It would be a distribution problem. Nomura was acting as intermediary and end holder, so if distribution was not working efficiently there would have to be lower prices to compensate."
Howard said while JGB yields were extremely unattractive at present levels, Japanese fundamentals were sound and the market may be worth a look for its defensive qualities.
"If the bond market rally should come to an end in the U.S....and 10-year yields go from 6.05 percent to 6.50 percent, Japan may well outperform significantly in that environment.
"We have a zero JGB weighting in our portfolios at the moment, but are wondering whether we should have a half weight. We're considering taking on board a JGB position as a risk reduction exercise."
Shah said there was very little reason to buy JGBs at current low yields, but said there may be a case for international investors to get into the market longer term.
"To put any new money in the market -- I'd say absolutely not," he said. "But from a currency perspective, an international perspective, it's different.
"Longer term dollar/yen is still heading to 105 so for international investors, JGBs may be a good buy at higher yields, purely on the back of potential currency appreciation."
The benchmark 182nd cash JGB yielded 2.115 in late Japanese trade, just off its April record low of 2.075 percent. Dollar/yen was at 118.20/30 by 1130 GMT.

Peter Wilson, yen analyst at Tokyo-Mitsubishi Finance, said JGB yields could fall because of the effect on the repo market, despite comments on Wednesday from Japan's Ministry of Finance that it could not rule out the possibility of a rise in market rates due to Nomura and DKB's exclusion from debt auctions.

"Nomura have been out of quite a few auctions already, and it hasn't had that effect. The opposite could happen -- the market will be a little bit short of paper if Nomura is kept out of the repo market, and that will have an impact on rates."
